title: Warnings Ignored, a Cup of Judgment
overview: After twenty-three years of unheeded warnings, Jeremiah announces that Babylon will overrun Judah and its neighbors for seventy years, and that every nation, Babylon included, will in turn face God's judgment.

parts.label: Twenty-three years unheard (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: This message is dated to the year Nebuchadnezzar became king of Babylon, when Jeremiah and other prophets had already been warning Judah for twenty-three years. Their message never changed: stop worshiping idols made by human hands and you can stay in your land, and in Hebrew the words for "turn" and "stay" sound almost alike.

parts.label: Babylon and seventy years (vv. 8-14)
parts.note: God calls Nebuchadnezzar "my servant," meaning the tool he will use to punish, not a worshiper, and ordinary life will fall silent: no wedding songs, no sound of millstones grinding grain, no lamp at night. Scholars differ on whether seventy years is an exact count or a round number for about a lifetime, and afterward Babylon itself will fall.

parts.label: The cup of God's anger (vv. 15-26)
parts.note: God's judgment is pictured as a cup of strong wine that makes nations stagger, most likely a vision or symbol rather than a real drink handed to kings. Jerusalem drinks first, then Egypt and the surrounding peoples, and last of all "Sheshak," widely understood as a coded name for Babylon made by swapping letters from opposite ends of the Hebrew alphabet.

parts.label: No one is exempt (vv. 27-29)
parts.note: If the nations refuse the cup, they must drink it anyway. The reasoning is blunt: if God does not spare his own city, no one else will be spared.

parts.label: The LORD roars like a lion (vv. 30-38)
parts.note: Harsh images pile up: a roaring lion, the shout of people stomping grapes, a storm crossing the world, and bodies left unburied on the ground. The "shepherds" are the rulers, wailing because the land they led is being destroyed.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the cup of judgment on all nations refers only to events in Jeremiah's own era or also points ahead to a final judgment of the world, as the book of Revelation's reuse of this imagery suggests to some.
think: When people hear the same warning for years and keep ignoring it, what do you think it would actually take for them to listen?
